coredata.dc:description: A series of novel quaternized benzylmethyl-containing poly(arylene ether nitrile)s (QPENs) were synthesized via condensation polymerization, bromination and quaternization. N,N,N′,N′-tetramethyl-1,6-diaminohexane dissolved in isopropanol was used as the quaternization reagent for the preparation of target anion exchange membranes (AEMs). 1H NMR spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) and gel permeation chromatography (GPC) were used to characterize the as-synthesized copolymers. The ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic segment on the polymer backbone was varied to study the structure–property of the AEMs. With strong nitrile dipole interchain interactions and a self-crosslinked structure, the resulting AEMs possess a self-anti-swelling property resulting in a low water uptake and swelling ratio. The AEMs show high ionic conductivity (under hydrated conditions) above the magnitude of 10−2 Scm−1. The membranes with distinct phase separation morphology have a higher ionic exchange capacity (IEC). The methanol permeability of the AEMs in the range 3.18–9.69×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 30°C and 8.92–25.57×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 60°C is lower than that of Nafion®117. The AEMs show an excellent alkaline stability in a 2M NaOH solution at 60°C for 1080h. A single cell with the QPEN membrane shows an open circuit voltage of 0.84V. A maximum power density of 79.1mWcm−2 at a current density of 207mAcm−2 can be achieved at 60°C. In summary the AEMs are good candidates for evaluation in fuel cells.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A series of novel quaternized benzylmethyl-containing poly(arylene ether nitrile)s (QPENs) were synthesized via condensation polymerization, bromination and quaternization. N,N,N′,N′-tetramethyl-1,6-diaminohexane dissolved in isopropanol was used as the quaternization reagent for the preparation of target anion exchange membranes (AEMs). 1H NMR spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) and gel permeation chromatography (GPC) were used to characterize the as-synthesized copolymers. The ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic segment on the polymer backbone was varied to study the structure–property of the AEMs. With strong nitrile dipole interchain interactions and a self-crosslinked structure, the resulting AEMs possess a self-anti-swelling property resulting in a low water uptake and swelling ratio. The AEMs show high ionic conductivity (under hydrated conditions) above the magnitude of 10−2 Scm−1. The membranes with distinct phase separation morphology have a higher ionic exchange capacity (IEC). The methanol permeability of the AEMs in the range 3.18–9.69×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 30°C and 8.92–25.57×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 60°C is lower than that of Nafion®117. The AEMs show an excellent alkaline stability in a 2M NaOH solution at 60°C for 1080h. A single cell with the QPEN membrane shows an open circuit voltage of 0.84V. A maximum power density of 79.1mWcm−2 at a current density of 207mAcm−2 can be achieved at 60°C. In summary the AEMs are good candidates for evaluation in fuel cells.

ce:section.ce:para: The development of fuel cells as efficient and environmentally benign power sources is currently drawn great attention globally because of increasing environmental concerns and a wish to disengage from the dependence of fossil fuels [1,2]. Of various fuel cell types, direct methanol fuel cells (DMFCs) have distinct advantages such as convenient transportation and storage of the fuels, compact design and low pollutant emission [3]. One of the most important components in DMFCs is polymer electrolyte membranes, which can be generally classified into proton exchange membranes (PEMs) and anion exchange membranes (AEMs). As a kind of PEMs, Nafion membranes are widely used in DMFCs, which exhibit excellent characteristics in ionic conductivity, chemical resistance and thermal stability. Nevertheless, those PEMs are also endowed with some drawbacks such as a low rate of methanol oxidation, high cost, and high methanol permeability at elevated temperature [4].

Consequently, there has been an increasing attention on AEMs since they have some advantages in DMFCs, which include: (1) the methanol oxidation rate is higher in alkaline media than in acid; (2) AEM-based alkaline DMFCs can use non-noble metal catalysts, such as Ag and Ni; (3) the methanol permeation is lower in alkaline media [5–7]. However, AEMs cannot be competitive with PEMs currently in terms of ionic conductivity and stability. Efforts have been devoted to developing novel AEM materials. Polymers with main chain structures such as poly(arylene ether sulfone) [8–10], polyetherketone [11,12], poly(ether imide) [13], poly(phenylene oxide) [14] and polymerized ionic liquid [15] have been used for AEM materials after modification by introducing hydroxide conducting groups such as quaternized ammonium, guanidinium, and imidazolium. However, those membranes tend to swell seriously at high humidity and temperature, especially with high ion content. As a result, the mechanical properties of the membranes decrease and the electrochemical performances become recessive.

Poly(arylene ether nitrile) (PEN) is a species of high-performance polymers that possess good mechanical properties, high thermal stability and chemical resistance [16]. Unlike many other polymers, PEN has strongly polar nitrile groups suspended on the benzene rings, which would probably promote the adhesion of the membrane to the catalyst layer in the membrane electrode assembly [17,18]. Furthermore, it has been reported that nitrile groups depressed the water uptake and membrane swelling because the dipole–dipole interaction force of nitrile groups increased the interchain interactions [19–22]. Gao et al. [23] prepared sulfonated poly(arylene ether nitrile) (SPEN) membranes for PEM fuel cells. The SPEN membranes exhibit lower water uptake and swelling ratio than sulfonated poly(aryl ether ketone) and poly(arylene ether sulfone) at a similar IEC. The proton conductivity of SPEN is approached to or even higher than that of Nafion®117, reaching 10−1 Scm−1. Kim et al. [24] also reported SPEN having high performance in DMFCs. These researches show the well potential applications of PEN materials for fuel cells.

To our knowledge, PEN materials have not been used for alkaline DMFCs. The objective of this work was thus to use PEN as a starting material to prepare AEMs for alkaline DMFCs. We synthesized a series of novel benzylmethyl-containing PENs followed by bromination to prepare PEN based AEMs. The brominated PENs were quaternized using N,N,N′,N′-tetramethyl-1,6-diaminohexane (TMHDA) to introduce quaternary ammonium groups into the benzyl groups. TMHDA is chosen because it has the longest carbon chain leading to the best alkaline stability in various diamines [25]. Then the as-prepared membranes were characterized. The structure–property relationship of the membranes was studied by varying the ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic segment.

4,4′-isopropylidenebis (2,6-dimethylphenol) (DMBHA) (98%, Aldrich, USA), 2,6-difluorobenzonitrile (DFBN) (99%, Aladdin, China), 4,4′-(hexafluoroisopropylidene) diphenol (BPHF) (98.0%, Aladdin, China) and TMHDA (98.0%, TCI, Japan) were used as received. Toluene and N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc) (98.0%, Sinopharm, China ) were stirred over CaH2 for 24h, then distilled under vacuum and stored over 4Å molecular sieves. Benzoyl peroxide (BPO) (99.0%, Sinopharm, China) was purchased from Tianjin Guangfu Fine Chemical Research Institute (China) and purified by recrystallizing from chloroform. All other chemicals were supplied from Shanghai Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (China) and used without further purification.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Synthesis of benzylmethyl-containing poly(arylene ether nitrile) (MPEN)
ce:section.ce:para: The precursor MPEN is synthesized by condensation polymerization, as shown in Scheme 1. A typical process for the synthesis of MPEN-x is detailed below, where x represents the molar ratio of DMBHA to DFBN. For example, sample MPEN-0.6 contains 0.6mol of DMBHA and 0.4mol of BPHF per 1.0mol of DFBN. 1.706g (6mmol) of DMBHA, 1.345g (4mmol) of BPHF, 1.391g (10mmol) of DFBN, 3.455g (25mmol) of K2CO3, 30mL of DMAc and 15mL of toluene were added into a 100mL three-necked flask with a magnetic stirrer, a Dean-Stark apparatus, and a gas inlet and outlet. The mixture was heated to 145°C under nitrogen for 4h. Meanwhile, the toluene and the water formed an azeotrope which was removed from the flask. Then the temperature was increased slowly to 165°C for another 20h. During this time, additional DMAc was charged to dilute the reaction system to prevent the solution from becoming too viscous to stir. Afterwards, the solution was cooled to room temperature (RT) and poured into 200mL of an aqueous methanol solution under stirring (methanol/deionized water=1/1, v/v) to produce a white solid precipitate. It was magnetically stirred at 80°C for another 5h, collected by filtration, Soxhlet extracted with methanol for 12h and dried at 80°C under vacuum for 24h to yield a pale white solid product.

The bromination reaction of MPEN was taken place in 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane (TCE), using N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) as the bromination agent and benzoyl peroxide (BPO) as the initiator. A typical procedure was as follows: 1.0g of MPEN-0.6 and 20mL of TCE were added into a 100mL three-necked round-bottomed flask equipped with a condenser, a magnetic stirrer, and a gas inlet and outlet. The mixture was heated to 85°C in a nitrogen atmosphere, and 1.185g (6.66mmol) of NBS and 0.081g (0.33mmol) of BPO were added after the polymer was dissolved completely. The reaction was proceeded at 85°C for 5h. The solution was poured into 200mL of methanol after cooling to RT. The resulting product was collected by filtration, Soxhlet extracted with methanol for 12h, and dried at RT under vacuum for 24h to yield a yellow solid (1.116g, 82% yield). The product is termed BPEN-0.6, where B denotes the bromination reaction.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Membrane formation, quaternization and alkalization of BPEN
ce:section.ce:para: The quaternized membranes were synthesized by SN2 substitution reaction to aminate the bromomethyl groups. A typical procedure was as follows: 1.000g of BPEN-0.6 was dissolved in 25mL of TCE followed by filtration using a 0.45µm PTFE membrane filter. The solution was cast onto clean glass plates and treated under vacuum at RT for 24h to obtain transparent membranes that were 25±2µm in thickness. The membranes were then soaked in a solution of TMHDA diluted by isopropyl alcohol (IPA) (v/v, 1:3) at 30°C for 48h. The quaternized membranes were thus obtained and washed repeatedly with IPA for 3h to remove excess TMHDA. After that the membranes were soaked in a 1M NaOH solution at RT for 24h to gain the OH− form membranes. The membranes were washed with deionized water for several times and kept in deionized water for more than 24h before use. The resulting membranes are termed QPEN-0.6, where Q denotes the quaternization reaction.

1H NMR spectra were acquired on an Avancell 500MHz spectrometer (Bruker, Switzerland). Deuterated chloroform (CDCl3-d) was used as the solvent and tetramethylsilane (TMS) as the internal standard. FT-IR spectra of the polymer and AEM samples were recorded in the range 500–4000cm−1 with an accumulation of 32 scans on a Nicolet Avatar 330 spectrophotometer (Thermo Electron Corporation, USA). Before testing, the polymers were dissolved in TCE to form a homogeneous solution and then cast onto clean glass plates under vacuum at RT for 24h to obtain colorless and transparent membranes.

The molecular weights of the polymers were measured using a GPC (Waters, USA) equipped with a Waters 1515 isocratic HPLC pump, a Waters 2414 refractive index detector (set to 30°C) and three Styragel columns (Waters HT4, HT5E and HT6). Tetrahydrofuran (THF) was used as the eluent with a flow rate of 1.0mLmin−1. Molecular weight was calibrated with standard polystyrene samples.

The SEM image of the membranes was recorded using a scanning electron microscope (S-4800, Hitachi, Japan). The samples were fractured in liquid nitrogen and then sputtered with gold before observation.

A thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA, SDQT600, TA, USA) was used to evaluate the thermal stability of the membranes. The samples were heated from 30 to 650°C with a rising rate of 10°Cmin−1 under a nitrogen atmosphere. The samples were dried at 60°C under vacuum for 48h before evaluation.

The WU of the membranes was determined using a quartz spring balance. Before measurement, the membranes were dried at 60°C under vacuum for 48h. The original length of the quartz spring was termed L 1. The length stretched to L 2 when the dried membrane was loaded. The membrane loaded quartz spring was hanged on a ground glass stopper which was fixed on the top of an inner glass cylinder with a sealed bottom. 50mL of deionized water was added into the bottom and heated to form a stable and saturated vapor pressure at a certain temperature. The temperature of the system was controlled by circulating water between the outer and the inner glass cylinders. The alkaline stability of the AEMs was evaluated by soaking the samples in a 2M NaOH solution at 60°C for different times from 24 to 1080h. Before testing, the AEMs were washed with deionized water for several times and immersed in deionized water for more than 24h.

A universal testing machine (WDW-1E Testing System) was used to characterize the mechanical property of the AEMs with a tensile speed of 10mmmin−1 at RT and 60% RH. A 15mm wide membrane was clipped and immersed in deionized water at RT for 24h and was taken out to wipe the surface water with a tissue before testing.

TEM images of the AEMs were recorded using a JEM-1230 electron microscope (JEOL, Japan) at a working voltage of 120kV. The membrane sample was first soaked into a 1.0M aqueous solution of sodium tungstate for 24h to stain with tungstate ions. Then the sample was washed repeatedly with deionized water and dried at 60°C under vacuum for 24h. After that the membrane was imbedded in an epoxy resin and sliced into a 60nm thick section by a microtome, and then placed on a copper grid for observation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Membrane electrode assembly (MEA) and fuel cell performance
ce:section.ce:para: The membrane electrode assembly (MEA) was made by the method reported in the literature [9]. Pt/C (40wt% Pt, Johnson Matthey) and the ionomer solution (OH− form, 5wt% in DMF) were mixed in propylene glycol under ultrasonic dispersion for 1h and vigorously stirred for 24h to prepare a homogeneous cathode catalyst ink. Then the catalyst ink was coated repeatedly on a Teflon-treated carbon paper (Toray-250) to prepare a cathode catalyst layer. The ionomer content and Pt loading were controlled at 30wt% and 1mgcm−2 in the catalyst layer, respectively. The resulting active electrode area was 4cm2. An anode catalyst layer was prepared by the same way using Pt–Ru/C (30wt% Pt, Johnson Matthey) as the anode catalyst. The cathode and anode catalyst layers were then placed in the two sides of the AEM and hot-pressed at 50°C and 1MPa for 5min. The single cell testing was performed at 60°C and 100% RH under atmospheric pressure on an electronic load (ZY8714, ZHONGYING Electronic Co., Ltd.) with serpentine flow channels. During the testing, the anode was fed with a 1M methanol solution and a 1M NaOH solution at a flow rate of 50mLmin−1 and the cathode was fed with air at a flow rate of 100mLmin−1.

A series of benzylmethyl-containing PENs (MPEN-0.4, MPEN-0.5, MPEN-0.6, MPEN-0.8 and MPEN-1.0) and their brominated products (BPEN-0.4, BPEN-0.5, BPEN-0.6, BPEN-0.8 and BPEN-1.0) were synthesized. Their chemical structure and molecular weight were determined by 1H NMR and GPC, respectively (
Figs. 1–3, and Table 1).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Synthesis and characterization of MPEN and BPEN
ce:section.ce:para: Benzylmethyl-containing PENs with different molar percentages of benzylmethyl groups were synthesized under various feed molar ratios of DMBHA/BPHF (0.4:0.6, 0.5:0.5, 0.6:0.4, 0.8:0.2 and 1.0:0) by polycondensation. The polymerization was proceeded smoothly and high molecular weight products (Mn>68,000gmol−1) were achieved.

Fig. 1a shows the 1H NMR spectrum of MPEN-0.6 as a typical example, in which all of the aromatic protons are assigned to the proposed polymer structure. In the aromatic region, the peaks around 7.47 and 6.98ppm could be assigned to the protons on benzene ring (f and b in Fig. 1a). The integration of the protons on positions b and f gives x=0.61. The peak at 7.28ppm is associated with CDCl3. The peaks around 1.71 and 2.18ppm are assigned to the chemical shifts of the protons on methyl (c in Fig. 1a) and benzyl (a in Fig. 1a), respectively.

Fig. 1b shows the 1H NMR spectrum of BPEN-0.6. After the bromination of MPEN, new peaks around 4.27–4.66ppm assigned to the methylene protons of the bromomethyl groups (m in Fig. 1b) are observed, and absent from the 1H NMR spectrum of MPEN-0.6 (Fig. 1a). Meanwhile, the peak associated with the benzyl (a in Fig. 1a and b) decreased in size after bromomethylation. Successful synthesis of BPEN-0.6 via the bromination on the MPEN is thus confirmed. The degree of bromomethylation of the BPEN can be calculated from the ratio of the integral area of –CH2Br to the sum of –CH3 and –CH2Br, as shown in Table 1.

Typically, MPEN-1.0 contains only the segment of tetramethylbisphenol A. In the 1H NMR spectrum of MPEN-1.0 (Fig. 2), the peaks around 7.15, 6.98 and 6.11ppm could be ascribed to the protons (e, b and d in Fig. 2) on benzene ring, respectively. The peak at 2.18ppm is attributed to the chemical shifts of the protons on benzyl (a in Fig. 2). The peak at 1.71ppm is assigned to the methyl protons (c in Fig. 2). These results indicate that the target polymers have been prepared successfully and the subsequent modification on the polymers is also feasible.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Membrane formation, quaternization and FT-IR spectrum
ce:section.ce:para: The AEMs were prepared by heterogeneous amination in which quaternization occurred when the membrane was cast in a nonionic form and subsequently converted to an ionic form in a solid state by introduction of TMHDA into the membrane. Fig. 3 shows the FT-IR spectra of MPEN-0.6, BPEN-0.6 and QPEN-0.6. For MPEN-0.6, the characteristic symmetric stretching band of nitrile groups is observed at 2232cm−1, and the peak at 1245cm−1 is assigned to phenoxy groups. Successful synthesis of the MPEN is thus confirmed. The new peak at 646cm−1 assigned to C–Br bond could be observed in the spectrum of BPEN-0.6. This suggests that bromine groups are successfully introduced into MPEN-0.6. For QPEN-0.6, the peak at 1669cm−1 assigned to C–N bond and the broad absorption peak around 3416cm−1 attributed to the stretching vibrations of –OH bond can be observed. These are absent from the spectrum of BPEN-0.6. The peak ascribed to the C–Br bond vanishes from QPEN-0.6 as well. This confirms the successful introduction of quaternary ammonium groups into BPEN-0.6.

ce:section.ce:section-title: IEC, water uptake (WU), swelling ratio of the membranes
ce:section.ce:para: The IEC of the AEMs reveals the number of exchangeable ion groups. The theoretical value of IEC is calculated from the polymer composition and the degree of bromination with the assumption that all the benzyl bromide groups are converted to benzyltrimethylammoniun groups and all the bromide ions are exchanged for hydroxide ions. The experimental value of IEC was gained by the titration method. As listed in Table 2, the theoretical values of IEC are in the range of 1.87–3.31meqg−1, and the experimental values are 1.56–2.51meqg−1. A comparison of the theoretical values with the experimental ones reveals that 73–83% benzyl bromide can be converted to quaternary ammonium groups in hydroxide form. This is probably that the quaternization process took place within the solid membranes rather than in liquid solutions, and the benzyl bromide groups cannot come into contact with TMHDA adequately [28].

Water molecules within the AEMs can dissociate the alkali functionality and facilitate the hydroxide ions transport. However, excessive water uptake can induce an undesirable dimensional deformation and suffer from a failure in mechanical strength. Therefore, maintaining water content in the membranes at a proper level is necessary to ensure mechanical properties. As listed in Table 2, both the water uptake and swelling ratio of the QPEN increased with increasing IEC and temperature. For example, by increasing the number of ammonium hydroxide groups, the water uptake increased from 15.91% to 35.65% at 30°C and from 26.26% to 54.57% at 60°C, and the swelling ratio increased from 9.18% to 24.77% at 30°C and from 15.85% to 41.63% at 60°C. For a better comparison of the membranes with different IECs, the number of absorbed water molecules per quaternary ammonium group (designated as λ) was calculated (Table 2). As shown in Table 2, λ for the QPEN membranes is in the range of 5.67–7.89 at 30°C and 9.35–12.08 at 60°C.

In comparison with the currently reported AEMs composed of aromatic polymers bearing quaternized ammonium groups [9,29–32], the QPEN membranes with a similar IEC are found to have a much lower water uptake and swelling ratio. On one hand, the presence of strong nitrile dipole interchain interactions tends to constrain swelling [19–22]. As one of the most polar functional groups, nitrile has a high dipole moment of ~3.9 Debyes. The strong polar nitrile groups in the QPEN obviously enhance the intra/intermolecular interaction. According to Kim׳s model [17], strong interchain polar nitrile–nitrile interactions could lead to an ideal combination of high IEC and low swelling. On the other hand, two types of crosslinking reaction occurred are also responsible for such low water uptake and swelling ratio, as noted by Zhao [33] and Wang [34]. As shown in Scheme 2, some TMHDA crosslinked with the polymer chain during quaternization. And after the quaternization some residual benzyl–bromide groups are still on the polymer chain. The Ar–CH2Br groups have enough activity to attack the highly active aromatic ring via Friedel–Crafts electrophilic substitution C-alkylation reaction [33]. During vacuum drying, those residual benzyl–bromide groups were crosslinked with benzene rings on other polymer chains to form methylene bonds. The interchain spacing of the polymer was thus reduced in the self-crosslinked structure. As a result, the free volume for water adsorption and storage in the QPEN membranes decreased, thereby reducing the water uptake. Consequently the dimensional stability of the membranes was improved.

The mechanical properties of the QPEN membranes were studied at RT and 60% RH, as shown in Table 3. The AEMs show tensile strengths varying from 21.48 to 31.43MPa and strain ranging from 8.35% to 15.06%. The AEMs with lower IEC show higher mechanical strength. These results are reasonable taking into account the higher IEC because higher water absorbability leads to a higher swelling.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ionic conductivity, methanol permeability and selectivity
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 4 shows the temperature dependence of the ionic conductivity of the AEMs and Nafion®117. The ionic conductivity of the membranes steadily increased with temperature because of the enhanced water mobility and ionic conductance [29]. In general, the conductivity above 10−2 Scm−1 is required for the application of AEM materials in alkaline fuel cells [35]. It can be seen that all the as-prepared AEMs show the conductivity above the magnitude of 10−2 Scm−1 over the entire temperature range and their conductivities increase with IEC values. Of those AEMs, QPEN-1.0 shows a highest conductivity of 5.06×10−2 Scm−1 at 30°C and 11.84×10−2 Scm−1 at 80°C. This is attributed to the sufficient hydrophilic groups in the AEMs. In conclusion, the as-prepared AEMs can be used for DMFCs in terms of ionic conductivity.

Membranes intended for DMFCs must have high ionic conductivity and be an effective barrier for methanol crossover from the anode to the cathode compartment. As shown in Table 2, the methanol permeability of the QPEN membranes is in the range of 3.18–9.69×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 30°C and 8.92–25.57×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 60°C, which are approximately one to two orders of magnitudes lower than that of Nafion®117 (obtained under the same condition in our laboratory). The methanol permeability of the QPEN membranes increased with the hydrophilic segment. This is because the imparted hydrophilicity contributes to increasing liquid uptake and methanol permeability and thus causing broadening of the ion-conducting channels.

To estimate the performance of the QPEN membranes on DMFCs, the selectivity defined as the ratio of the ionic conductivity to the methanol permeability was calculated. The relative selectivity, which is defined as the ratio of the selectivity of the QPEN membranes to that of Nafion®117, is also estimated as shown in Fig. 5. The relative selectivity of all the as-prepared membranes is higher than that of Nafion®117 at 60°C. With the lowest value, the relative selectivity of QPEN-0.4 is still nine times higher than that of Nafion®117. With an excellent resistance to methanol, the QPEN membranes are potential for DMFCs.

In order to get an in-depth understanding of the anion conductive behavior of membranes, the AEMs were examined by TEM to provide an illuminating insight into the ordering and size of ion domains in the AEMs. The TEM images of QPEN-0.4, QPEN-0.6, QPEN-0.8 and QPEN-1.0 are shown in Fig. 6. The bright and dark regions in the images correspond to the unstained hydrophobic domains and the tungstate ion-stained electron-rich hydrophilic domains, respectively.

As shown in Fig. 6a–d, a homogeneous distribution of the hydrophilic/hydrophobic phases is observed in the QPEN membranes because the polymer is randomly composed of hydrophilic and hydrophobic repeating units. By increasing IEC, obvious ion clusters can be formed leading to distinct phase separation morphology in the AEM. This might be favorable for ion transport and conductivity. Ion clusters can be observed in QPEN-0.8 (ca. 1–1.5nm in diameter) and QPEN-1.0 (ca. 2–3nm in diameter). For QPEN-1.0, the ion clusters were interconnected in some regions. It is considered that the presence of strongly polar nitrile groups obviously enhances the aggregation of the quaternary ammonium groups with high polarity and flexibility. The quaternary ammonium groups which have long carbon chain in the QPEN copolymers were anchored densely onto the 4,4′-isopropylidene bis (2,6-dimethylphenol) monomers to facilitate the formation of ion domains [36]. By combining the microscopic observation with ion-conducting behavior, one concludes that larger ion domains and higher density of ion clusters in AEMs lead to a higher ionic conductivity.

The cross-sectional SEM image of QPEN-0.6 is shown in Fig. 7a. A uniform and smooth structure with approximately 26μm in thickness can be clearly observed. Fig. 7b shows the surface morphology of QPEN-0.6. A homogeneous and dense target membrane is thus confirmed. Smooth surface of the AEMs will enhance an effective contact leading to a high catalytic efficiency. The densification of the AEMs can be effective barriers for methanol. Therefore the QPEN membranes can exhibit good performances in DMFCs because of the high catalytic efficiency and the good methanol-resistance.

The thermal degradation behavior of the QPEN membranes was studied via TGA. As can be seen in Fig. 8, the decomposition process of the as-prepared membranes can be divided into three steps: (1) all of the membranes show an initial weight loss between 30 and 160°C which is attributed to the evaporation of the bonded water and the residual solvent (TCE). (2) The second weight loss from 190 to 380°C is assigned to the decomposition of the quaternary ammonium salt groups and the breakage of the new bonds formed from the self-crosslinking reaction [33]. (3) The third weight loss from nearly 400°C is ascribed to the cleavage of the polymer main chain. In general, all of the QPEN membranes exhibit good thermal stability in an intermediate temperature range.

The alkaline stability of the QPEN membranes was evaluated by soaking the AEMs in a 2M NaOH solution at 60°C. As shown in Fig. 9, an initial sharp decrease for both the AEMs was observed after the membrane being soaked within 250h. After that, the ionic conductivity tended to be a constant value. The ionic conductivity of QPEN-0.8 and QPEN-1.0 decreased by 32% and 37% respectively after testing for more than 1000h. The performance of the AEM with both hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments was improved over the AEM with sole hydrophilic segments. Furthermore, the ionic conductivity of both the AEMs is still found to be greater than the magnitude of 10−2 Scm−1. Furthermore, we also measured the variation in IEC of the AEMs. After the alkaline stability test, the IEC of QPEN-0.8 and QPEN-1.0 changed from 2.20 to 1.67meqg−1 and 2.51 to 1.75meqg−1, respectively.

A great attention has been given on the alkaline stability of the nitrile groups. The hydrolysis of nitriles groups can yield carboxylic acids, as noted by Du et al. [37]. Therefore, the AEMs were further structurally analyzed by comparing their FT-IR spectra before and after the alkaline stability evaluation to determine whether there was any hydrolysis of the nitrile groups, as shown in Fig. 10. No significant changes of the peak at 2232cm−1 associated with the nitrile groups in their FT-IR spectra were observed, indicating that the integrity of the nitrile groups was maintained. One reason for it maybe that the conditions for this test have not met the requirements for the hydrolysis of the nitrile groups.

1H NMR is also used to determine whether there is any hydrolysis of the nitrile group. The 1H NMR of the QPEN membranes before and after the alkaline stability test cannot be provided because the QPEN membranes cannot be dissolved by any D-substituted solvents due to their self-crosslinked structure. Instead, PEN-0.8 was used as an alternative to test the alkaline stability in a 2M NaOH solution at 60°C for 140h. The 1H NMR spectra of PEN-0.8 before and after the alkaline stability test are shown in Fig. 11. No significant changes in the 1H NMR spectra were observed. This indicates that the hydrolysis of the nitrile groups is negligible under such condition. Other nitrile-containing AEMs were also reported to possess high chemical stability in alkaline solutions [38,39].
A considerable amount of the ionic conductivity and IEC remained shows that the QPEN membranes have excellent alkaline stability for DMFC applications.

The QPEN-0.8 membrane is used for a single cell test given it has the highest ratio of ionic conductivity to methanol permeability. For a single cell equipped with QPEN-0.8 operated at 60°C and 1atm with 100% RH, the polarization and power density−current density relationship curves are shown in Fig. 12. An open circuit voltage (OCV) of 0.84V and a maximum power density of 79.1mWcm−2 can be achieved at a current density of 207mAcm−2. Without optimization, the peak power density was much higher than the reported PEMs based on cardo poly(arylene ether nitrile)s (21.5mWcm−2) [40] for DMFCs. The acceptable cell performance is resulting from the high conductivity of the QPEN-0.8 membrane. Moreover, the methanol oxidation is faster and the migration of hydroxyl ions is in the opposite direction of the methanol permeation in the alkaline conditions, this would effectively reduce the voltage loss caused by fuel permeation [5–7]. Furthermore, the strong dipole forces of the nitrile groups suspended on the polymer chains potentially promote the adhesion of the membrane to the catalyst layer resulting in an improved quality of MEAs [17,18].

In summary, we successfully synthesized a series of novel quaternized benzylmethyl-containing PEN AEMs by polycondensation, benzylmethyl conversion, and quaternization. TMHDA was used to introduce the exchange groups. The IEC of the AEMs is in between 1.56 and 2.51meqg−1 and the corresponding structure dependence of water uptake varied within the range 15.91–35.65% at 30°C and 26.26–54.57% at 60°C. The strong nitrile dipole interchain interactions and self-crosslinked structure of the membranes are responsible for their very low water uptake and swelling ratio. By increasing IEC, the membranes reveal distinct phase separation morphology. The ionic conductivity of the membranes increased with IEC and temperature, and was in the range of 1.34–11.84×10−2 Scm−1. The methanol permeability of the AEMs in the range 3.18–9.69×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 30°C and 8.92–25.57×10−8 cm2 s−1 at 60°C is much lower than that of Nafion®117. Single cell testing using QPEN-0.8 showed an open circuit voltage of 0.84V and a maximum power density of 79.1mWcm−2 at 60°C. The membranes also showed good thermal, alkaline stability and mechanical properties. These results suggest that the new AEMs produced in this study are promising for application in DMFCs. All of the data were obtained by averaging more than three experimental values, and the errors were less than 5%.
